chapter.title: Three Languages
chapter.sub: Three languages, one stream, human captions — and at rehearsal, two languages on the English track.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 7 · EPISODE 8 · DRAFT  Leadership summit · Maya, Adaeze, Luis and the interpreters · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  Three languages, one stream to forty sites, and human captions. At the rehearsal, the English track has two languages on it — and so does the captioner.  ⚑ RV-155: interpreters’ working conditions are theirs; captions are an access requirement; languages invented. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Three Languages
items.stakes: Three languages, one stream, human captions — and at the rehearsal, two languages on the English track.
items.clock: Before Thursday's summit opens at 09:00 in Valmera.
items.reward: Every listener, in the room or on the stream, hears one language all day.

objectives.text: Decide how to find what's mixed
Decide what happens during the Tahvaran speech
Decide what the events standard says

items.rumor: One channel. One language. Every listener.

items.alt: The Valmera auditorium at rehearsal: two lit interpretation booths at the back; Adaeze on the phone to Tahvara; Maya with a hand to her headphones.

bubbles.text: Tahvara hears Valmeran under the English. And the captioner says her feed has two languages.

items.caption: Two days to the summit.

lines.text: Tahvara says track one is English with Valmeran underneath. And the captioner's quitting in ten minutes if it doesn't stop.
Then let's listen to exactly what she's getting.

items.text: Act I — “Two voices on track one”

items.prompt: 15:10. The captioner is about to walk out. What do you do first?
items.happening: Two languages on track 1 and the captioner's feed.
items.risk: Forty sites hearing two languages — and captions that help nobody.
timeout: Wednesday's check finds the same patch.

hints.text: What exactly is each listener hearing, and where does it come from?

options.label: Turn the Valmeran level down on track 1
options.result: Quieter, still there. The captions still stumble.
options.consequence: Less of the wrong thing is still the wrong thing.

options.label: Put on headphones and listen to each track and the captioner's feed, then trace each back to the bus it comes from
options.result: Track 1 and the captioner both come from the sound engineer's booth-monitor bus.
options.consequence: Hear what each listener hears; find the source.

options.label: Switch the stream to automatic captions
options.result: The accessibility lead: “Human captions are the policy for this event.”
options.consequence: Replaces an access requirement to hide a patching error.

options.label: Ask the interpreters to speak more quietly
options.result: The lead interpreter: “We're not the problem. Your patch is.”
options.consequence: Blaming the people doing it right.
options.fail: Don't make the interpreters fix the system.

items.title: Two voices on track one.
items.body: The sound engineer built a booth-monitor bus — floor plus Valmeran — so he could hear the booth and the floor at once. His patch sheet sends stream track 1 and the captioner's feed from it too. A mix for checking had become a channel for listening.
items.label: Test: what was on track 1 — and how much of the summit is the Tahvaran speech?

items.alt: A channel sheet: Track 1 English and the captioner both fed floor plus Valmeran, in red; tracks 2 and 3 correct; below, in red: the Tahvaran speech has no retour and no relay.
items.caption: A checking mix, sent to listeners.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Adaeze beside a board. Three languages, three stream tracks. What must each track carry? One language each — the floor on one, each booth on its own. Three at a hundred and twenty-eight kilobits is three hundred and eighty-four. And track one feeds the captions. If track one carries two languages, so do the captions.

bubbles.text: Three languages, three stream tracks. What must each track carry?
One language each — the floor on one, each booth on its own. Three at a hundred and twenty-eight kilobits is three hundred and eighty-four.
And track one feeds the captions. If track one carries two languages, so do the captions.

items.caption: Advanced: the formula is there if you ask. Try without it first.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Simultaneous interpretation   Relay (interpretation)   Interpretation booth   CART captioning   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Uncompressed bit rate   ƒ FORMULA · Uncompressed bit rate  R = channels × f s  × b   f s   sample rate, Hz  b  bits per sample  R  bits per second (÷ 1,000,000 for Mbit/s)      ƒ Ask for the formula · Counting combinations   ƒ FORMULA · Counting combinations  total = a × b   a, b  the two things being multiplied (e.g. presets × outputs)

items.label: **Learn it now:** interpretation, relay and captions.

items.label: **Fix it:** one language per track — for the stream and the captioner.

items.title: The relay.
items.body: Item 6 on the running order: the Tahvaran regional director, twenty minutes, in Tahvaran. Booth V works from English, not Tahvaran. The design wired the English channel to the floor — so during her speech the English track and the captions would carry Tahvaran, and the Valmeran channel would go silent. Nobody had planned for booth T to work back into English, or for booth V to take relay from it.
items.label: Test: what would each channel carry — and whose decision is the plan?

items.prompt: Wednesday morning. How is the Tahvaran speech handled?
items.happening: A 20-minute speech in Tahvaran; no retour, no relay.
known: ◉ Booth V doesn't work from Tahvaran
◉ English channel wired to the floor
items.risk: Twenty minutes of silence on one channel and the wrong language on another.
timeout: The question waits for the morning of the summit.
The Valmeran channel goes silent at 10:40.

hints.text: Who decides how the booths work — and what paths do they need?

options.label: Ask the director to give her speech in English
options.result: Her office: “She speaks for her region in its language. That's the point of the summit.”
options.consequence: Takes a speaker's language to fix a routing gap.
options.fail: Fix the system, not the speaker.

options.label: With the interpreters and the events team: booth T works into English during her speech (retour) on the English channel; booth V takes relay from it; track 1 and the captions follow the English channel; rehearse the switch with both booths this afternoon
options.result: The lead interpreters agree the plan; the sound engineer adds the relay input; the afternoon rehearsal switches cleanly both ways.
options.consequence: Their craft, the system's paths, rehearsed together.

options.label: Let the Valmeran channel go quiet for twenty minutes
options.result: A third of the room hears nothing while a director speaks.

options.label: Publish a translated transcript next week
options.result: Useful afterwards — no help in the room.

items.title: Four languages at once
items.body: Simultaneous interpretation — interpreters speaking while the speaker speaks, into headphones for listeners who choose a language — was tried in the late 1920s and made its name at the Nuremberg trials of 1945–46, where English, French, Russian and German ran at once through wired headsets. The interpreters worked in shifts, and the system's first rule was that every listener chose one language.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #69 · AVERY'S LENS  One channel, one language  Every listener picks one channel and must hear exactly one language on it — including the captioner, who is a listener too.  Track 1 carried English with Valmeran underneath, and so did the captioner's feed. Remote viewers heard two languages; the captions tried to write both.

items.alt: Thursday, during the Tahvaran director's speech: the auditorium full, both booths working; Maya at the back with headphones; Luis beside her.

bubbles.text: Channel one: English, from booth T. Channel two: Valmeran, on relay. Captions still running.
Three languages. And nobody noticed the switch.

items.prompt: I've never run interpretation. What do I need to know by Thursday?

options.label: “That the interpreters decide how they work. We give them a clean floor, their own channel, relay when they need it — and we ask before we change anything.”
options.reply: So I start by asking them. Right.

options.label: “It's just three audio channels.”
options.reply: Three channels, six interpreters and a captioner who's already angry. ‘Just.’

options.label: “Which languages can each booth work from?”
options.reply: Good question. I… don't know. I'll ask.

items.title: TRK1 ← MON B
items.body: The sound engineer's patch sheet: ‘TRK1 ← MON B · CART ← MON B’. MON B was his booth-check bus — floor plus Valmeran, so he could hear both at once. Nobody meant the stream to hear it.

items.alt: The channel sheet after the fix: track 1 English and the captioner from the floor, track 2 booth V, track 3 booth T, all green; during the Tahvaran speech booth T works into English and booth V takes relay.
items.caption: One channel, one language, all day.

items.title: 10:40 · in Tahvaran
items.body: The summit's running order, item 6: ‘10:40 — Regional director, Tahvara (in Tahvaran), 20 min.’ The interpretation brief listed English → Valmeran and English → Tahvaran. Nothing the other way.

items.prompt: After the summit. What goes into the events standard?
known: ◉ The plan lived in one afternoon's notes
items.risk: The same two voices next year.
timeout: The notes stay on the sound engineer's laptop.

hints.text: What would next year's crew need to know on day one?

options.label: Nothing — it went well
options.result: Next year's summit has a new sound engineer and a new patch.
options.consequence: The lesson leaves with this crew.

options.label: An interpretation plan for every multilingual event: languages each booth works from and into, relay and retour paths, a clean undelayed floor to the booths, one language per track, the captioner on the English channel, and a check with the interpreters before doors
options.result: The events team adopts it; the interpreters ask for a copy for other clients.
options.consequence: Written with the people who do the work.

options.label: Drop interpretation from future summits
options.consequence: Removes the access to remove the risk.

options.label: Let each region stream its own language separately
options.result: Three streams, three budgets, no shared room.
options.consequence: Splits the summit instead of serving it.

items.alt: The empty auditorium after the summit; the booths dark. Adaeze holding a printed thank-you card from the interpreters.

bubbles.text: The captioner sent a thank-you. So did the interpreters. Nobody's ever thanked me for a patch.
You asked them first. That's what they're thanking.

items.alt: The executive floor; Henrik holding a thick binder labelled ROOM STANDARD v2 · 140 CLAUSES, with sticky notes from every region.

bubbles.text: The board wants Standard v3 by the end of the quarter. Every region has sent me its wish list.

items.caption: Next: *Standard v3.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  One channel, one language — for every listener, the captioner included. Feed tracks and captions from clean buses, never from a monitoring mix. Give interpreters a clean, undelayed floor, and plan relay and retour with them for every language on the running order. R = channels × f s  × b. Captions are an access requirement; the policy’s owner decides human or automatic.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Who is listening to something you produce that you’ve never asked about?
